short: A handful of unfinished Polish bunkers held up a panzer corps for three days.
full:
The fortified position at Wizna covered the crossing of the Narew river on the road to Bialystok and the northern flank of Warsaw. It was garrisoned by around 700 Polish troops under Captain Wladyslaw Raginis, with a few anti-tank guns and machine guns in concrete bunkers that had not been finished. From 7 September 1939 they faced Guderian's XIX Panzer Corps, some 40,000 men with several hundred tanks and heavy artillery.

The defence held for three days. Bunkers were reduced one at a time by direct fire, engineers and dive bombers, and by the morning of 10 September only one was still resisting. Raginis had sworn not to leave his position alive and killed himself with a grenade rather than surrender. The delay was small against the scale of the campaign, but it cost Guderian time on his drive south towards Brest. Almost unknown outside Poland for decades, Wizna is now commemorated there as a Polish Thermopylae.
